State the end goal and why it matters before describing the steps, so the model can make sensible judgment calls.
Name the audience and their expertise level so tone and depth match the reader.
Specify the output format explicitly: structure, sections, length, and whether to use markdown, JSON, or prose.
Put long reference material (documents, data, code) first, wrapped in descriptive XML tags, and the question or instruction after it.
Describe what a good result looks like with concrete success criteria rather than vague adjectives like 'good' or 'detailed'.
List hard constraints (must / must not) separately from preferences so the model can tell which can bend.
Tell the model what to do rather than only what not to do.
When the input may be ambiguous or missing information, tell the model how to handle it: ask, assume and state the assumption, or flag it.
For code tasks, give the language, version, framework, and how the result will be run or tested.
For analysis or reasoning tasks, ask the model to check its answer against the stated criteria before finishing.
Include one short example of the desired output when format matters, labelled as illustrative so it is not copied verbatim.
Use placeholders like [VARIABLE] for details only the user can supply instead of inventing them.
